title: Ramadan: the lanterns
hookLine: Cairo's Ramadan lanterns, a custom centuries old

lines: A NEW CAMP: THE HOLY DAYS.
cards: A Cairo alley, just after sunset, in the month of fasting. Strings of lights zigzag between balconies.

In a shop doorway hang lanterns in rows: tin frames punched with patterns, panes of red, green and blue glass, a little door on the side for the candle. A child walks past swinging a small one, singing.
Some newer ones are plastic and play a tune when you press a button. The old ones smell of hot metal and wax. The whole street glows like the inside of a jewel box.
A new camp starts today, the holy days in history, and it opens with one object. Today's word: fanous.

teach.b: First, the word. Fanous is the Arabic word for a lantern, and in Egypt it has come to mean the Ramadan lantern above all.

teach.h: A STORY OF LIGHTS FOR A RULER.
teach.b: Second, the story. People in Cairo tell of a Fatimid ruler who arrived in the city by night; the people came out carrying lanterns to light his way, and the lanterns stayed with the month.
Other versions put them in the hands of children, or of women walking out after dark in the fasting month. Nobody can prove which is true. What the stories agree on is light, and Ramadan nights.
Third, why light belongs here. The Qur'an names the month itself: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind." And elsewhere it gives a picture made of light.

teach.h: A LAMP IN A GLASS, IN A NICHE.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is as it were a shining star."
A lamp, in a glass, in a niche. Some readers hear that verse in the glow of a fanous. Fourth, the street.
Ramadan nights are busy: the meal at sunset, the night prayers, visits to family, a late walk.

teach.h: THE DARK STREET BECOMES A PLACE.
teach.b: The fanous turns the dark street into a place to be.

teach.h: ALLAH IS THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.
teach.b: Far from Egypt, some families hang one by the door, or set one on the iftar table, so the children know the month has come.

how: In Egypt and in some families elsewhere, Ramadan lanterns are hung in streets, shop doorways and homes for the month, and children carry small ones in the evenings.

games.q: you're in Cairo, and the ruler is arriving by night at the start of the fasting month. the streets are dark. what do you do, in the story people tell?
o: go out carrying lanterns to light his way.
games.why: in the story, the people came out with lanterns, and the lanterns stayed with Ramadan. it's a story, not a record.

practice: Light a candle or a lamp, or simply look at the nearest glow, a screen dimmed low, a streetlight through the window, and watch where its edge meets the dark. Let your breathing slow until the light seems steady.
If you pray, recall the verse of light, a lamp in a glass, in a niche; if not, just rest your eyes on the glow.

wordCard.voice: Fanous. The lantern, and in Egypt above all the Ramadan lantern of tin and colored glass, carried through the streets after sunset. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: lantern; in Egypt, the Ramadan lantern.
